cues.text: We now turn to additional Industry four point zero applications, and in particular to technical assistance.
Let us begin with that idea.
Technical assistance is a core characteristic of Industry four point zero.
It means that systems actively give people information and support while they work, rather than leaving operators to rely only on memory or experience.
The source names three forms.
The first is visual warnings, where a system draws attention to a problem, such as a display or signal showing that a machine is outside its safe range.
The second is augmented maintenance guidance, where a technician receives step-by-step help overlaid on or alongside the equipment they are repairing, so they can see what to do and in what order.
The third is decision aids, where the system presents information that helps a person choose between options.
In each case the system assists the human.
It does not simply replace the human.
This connects to a second characteristic, decentralised decision-making.
In an Industry four point zero setting, decisions can be made closer to where the work happens, by machines or by people at the point of action, instead of waiting for a central manager.
But the source is clear that this must remain within safety, authority and accountability limits.
In plain terms, someone must still be responsible, the decision must be one that the person or system is actually permitted to make, and it must never compromise safety.
Decentralised does not mean uncontrolled.
The third idea here is information transparency.
This means reliable shared information about physical assets and processes.
Think of a machine, a product batch or a production line, where the people who need to know its condition can see an accurate picture of it.
Be careful with the word transparency, though.
The source stresses that it does not mean unrestricted disclosure.
Information is shared with the right participants, for the right purpose, and reliably.
It is not made open to everyone.
Now let us look at three company examples.
Siemens smart-factory examples illustrate sensor-connected manufacturing and real-time quality monitoring.
Here the technology role is this: sensors connect machines and production steps, and quality can be watched as production happens, instead of being discovered afterwards.
Amazon fulfilment robotics illustrates coordinated warehouse movement and automation.
The technology role is robots moving in a coordinated way within a warehouse, automating the handling and movement of goods.
Nestlé's IoT quality and supply-chain examples illustrate traceability and the monitoring of product conditions.
The technology role is following a product through the supply chain and checking the conditions it experiences along the way.
The source asks us to use these as technology-role comparisons, not as proof of results.

That means we compare what kind of job the technology does in each case: sensing and quality monitoring for Siemens, coordinated automation for Amazon, and traceability and condition monitoring for Nestlé.
We should not claim any specific performance figure from them, because the source does not support one.
One further point follows from the supply-chain examples.
Supply-chain visibility requires three things across all participants.
First, shared identifiers, so that everyone refers to the same item, batch or shipment in the same way.
Second, timely events, meaning that updates about what has happened arrive soon enough to be useful.
Third, data standards, meaning agreed formats so that one participant's data can be understood by another.
Without these three, visibility breaks down at the boundaries between organisations.
Next, let us consider what the Internet of Things, or I-o-T, enables.
The source lists five uses.
Energy monitoring, where consumption is measured and tracked.
Proactive maintenance, where equipment condition is watched so that attention can be given before failure.
Quality optimisation, where measurements help improve the quality of output.
Risk and compliance monitoring, where conditions are checked against safety or regulatory expectations.
And usage-informed product improvements, where information about how customers actually use a product guides how it is improved.
To make this concrete, take a cold-chain sensor, the kind used to keep chilled or frozen goods at the right temperature.
Such a sensor can do three things.
It can record temperatures over time.
It can issue local warnings when something goes wrong.
And it can preserve an auditable history, so that afterwards someone can check what happened.
But the source is careful about the limits.
A cold-chain sensor cannot guarantee food quality if the sensors are uncalibrated or the records are incomplete.
An uncalibrated sensor may report temperatures that are wrong, and gaps in the record mean that you cannot be sure what happened during the missing periods.
So the technology alone is not enough.

The source tells us to design three things: alarm thresholds, which are the points at which a warning is triggered; responsible responders, meaning named people or roles who must act when an alarm sounds; and verification, which means checking that the sensors and the records can be trusted.
Finally, let us look ahead.

The source mentions potential future technologies: advanced edge AI, which places artificial intelligence closer to the device where data is produced; next-generation connectivity, meaning improved ways of connecting devices and systems; and quantum computing, for selected computational problems.
Note the qualification on quantum computing.
It is an emerging possibility, not an established, general-purpose tool for optimising factories.
We should not assume it is ready for everyday factory use.
The source also introduces Industry five point zero.
It emphasises three things: human-machine collaboration, sustainability and resilience.

Compared with a focus on automation alone, the stress is on people and machines working together, on environmental and long-term responsibility, and on the ability to withstand and recover from disruption.
The closing lesson is about leadership.

Before investing in any of these technologies, leaders must evaluate four things: maturity, meaning how proven and ready the technology is; cost; usefulness, meaning whether it solves a real problem for the organisation; and risk.
A promising technology is not automatically a sound investment.
Good digital leaders test it against these four questions first.
